figures.name: Verifiable evidence for AI and Physical AI
figures.alt: Four needs for AI and physical AI: grounded answers, provenance, SHACL-based data validation and change propagation, with a fictional humanoid test-report withdrawal example.
figures.description: Four needs for AI and physical AI: grounded answers, provenance, SHACL-based data validation and change propagation, with a fictional humanoid test-report withdrawal example.
figures.caption: Semantic grounding and provenance help AI systems use attributable product evidence. SHACL validates declared data constraints, not physical safety or permission to act. The robot-release HOLD example is fictional; a real result depends on verified dependencies, current evidence and enforcement. Adapted from the visual paper, page 25.
figures.credit_text: Dr. Carsten Stöcker / Spherity GmbH; standalone figure adapted from the visual paper

figures.name: DPP5.0 maturity ladder
figures.alt: Five levels of Spherity’s proposed DPP model: DPP1.0 document, DPP2.0 structured data, DPP3.0 semantics, DPP4.0 verifiable claims and DPP5.0 evidence graphs.
figures.description: Five levels of Spherity’s proposed DPP model: DPP1.0 document, DPP2.0 structured data, DPP3.0 semantics, DPP4.0 verifiable claims and DPP5.0 evidence graphs.
figures.caption: The Spherity DPP1.0–DPP5.0 maturity ladder separates documents, structured data, common semantics, verifiable claims and access-controlled evidence graphs. The EU Registry is positioned at the semantic stage for this analysis. These levels are research categories, not EU legal classifications. Adapted from the visual paper, page 26.
figures.credit_text: Dr. Carsten Stöcker / Spherity GmbH; standalone figure adapted from the visual paper

figures.name: DPP5.0: definition and seven properties
figures.alt: Seven DPP5.0 properties: graph evidence, issuer-bound verification, access control, open standards, open-world semantics, accountability and cross-organization sharing.
figures.description: Seven DPP5.0 properties: graph evidence, issuer-bound verification, access control, open standards, open-world semantics, accountability and cross-organization sharing.
figures.caption: DPP5.0 combines verifiable provenance, governed actor authority, explicit permission, extensible semantics and cross-organization evidence. A signed credential does not by itself prove truth or legal competence. This is a target definition, not an adopted EU/W3C profile. Adapted from the visual paper, page 27.
figures.credit_text: Dr. Carsten Stöcker / Spherity GmbH; standalone figure adapted from the visual paper

figures.name: Open standards stack: from semantics to organizational authority and policy
figures.alt: Five-layer proposed stack: DCAT catalogue, SKOS/SHACL/OWL meaning, JSON-LD/RDF evidence, W3C verifiable credentials/DIDs and European Business Wallet identity, and ODRL policy.
figures.description: Five-layer proposed stack: DCAT catalogue, SKOS/SHACL/OWL meaning, JSON-LD/RDF evidence, W3C verifiable credentials/DIDs and European Business Wallet identity, and ODRL policy.
figures.caption: The lower layers reflect semantic technologies present in the Commission DPP package. Credentials, organizational identity and policy are proposed extensions. EBW is a proposed EU framework, not a W3C standard; ODRL expresses policy but requires separate decision and enforcement. Adapted from the visual paper, page 32.
figures.credit_text: Dr. Carsten Stöcker / Spherity GmbH; standalone figure adapted from the visual paper
